cves.d: A flaw has been found in ONNX ONNXMLTools up to 1.16.0. This impacts the function visualize_model of the file onnxmltools/utils/visualize.py. This manipulation of the argument producer_name causes basic cross site scripting. The attack is possible to be carried out remotely. The exploit has been published and may be used. The pull request to fix this issue awaits acceptance.

Improper authentication in OIDC bearer token verification in Canonical LXD before 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows a remote attacker holding a token signed by the configured identity provider to authenticate to the LXD API and gain unauthorized control or impersonate users via presenting tokens issued for other applications, ID tokens, or unverified email claims.

Symbolic link following in imported VM backup config drive preparation in Canonical LXD before 4.0.16, 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows an authenticated user with project-scoped permissions to disclose sensitive host files, including LXD server and cluster keys, and overwrite host files as root via importing and starting a VM backup with a symlinked config directory.

A flaw was found in Keycloak. An offline session continues to be valid when the offline_access scope is removed from the client. The refresh token is accepted and you can continue to request new tokens for the session. As it can lead to a situation where an administrator removes the scope, and assumes that offline sessions are no longer available, but they are.

A vulnerability was found in perl 5.30.0 through 5.38.0. This issue occurs when a crafted regular expression is compiled by perl, which can allow an attacker controlled byte buffer overflow in a heap allocated buffer.

Improper link resolution before file access in recursive file pull in Canonical LXD before 4.0.15, 5.0.11, 5.21.9, and 6.8 on case-insensitive client filesystems allows an authenticated user with write access to an instance directory or custom volume to write arbitrary files outside the target directory and execute code as the operator via case-variant symlinks.

Improper certificate validation in websocket connections in Canonical pylxd before 2.4.3 allows a network attacker to read command stdin and spoof command output via impersonating a remote LXD endpoint.

Exposure of sensitive information in live and stateful migration operations in Canonical LXD before 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows an authenticated user with project event or operation read access to read a migrating instance's checkpointed runtime state and disrupt the migration via capturing the state connection secret from operation events or queries.

Exposure of sensitive information and missing requestor validation in instance, volume, and snapshot migration operations in Canonical LXD before 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows an authenticated user with project event or operation read access to read migrating configuration and filesystem data and disrupt the migration via capturing per-connection websocket secrets from operation metadata and racing the migration's data channels.

Exposure of resource to wrong sphere in VM disk migration, export, and attach NBD servers in Canonical LXD before 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows an unprivileged local user in the host network namespace to read and modify a guest VM's disk and execute code inside the guest via connecting to abstract Unix sockets while an operation is active.

Incorrect permission assignment for critical resources in rsync transfer sockets, instance storage directories, proxy socket paths, and disk staging mounts in Canonical LXD before 4.0.16, 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows an unprivileged local user to gain root privileges on the host, read or modify transferred volumes, alter host file permissions, and inject AppArmor rules via connecting to unauthenticated abstract Unix sockets, running setuid binaries, or racing path and mount operations.

Improper output encoding in Prometheus metrics exposition in Canonical LXD before 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows a user controlling a virtual machine to forge host metric labels and break metrics scraping via unescaped guest-controlled filesystem mountpoints and network interface names.

Authentication bypass by spoofing in bridged NIC MAC filtering in Canonical LXD before 4.0.16, 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows a privileged user inside an instance sharing a managed bridge to intercept and deny inbound network traffic addressed to a neighbour instance via sending frames with a spoofed source MAC address before filtering drops them.

In LXD before 5.21.0 and 6.10.0, an OS command injection vulnerability allows an authenticated client restricted to a single project to execute arbitrary code as root on the host.

 The raw.dnsmasq bridge network configuration key is not restricted to server administrators and is copied verbatim into the dnsmasq configuration file, so a user whose project keeps the default features.networks=false can have a bridge network created in the default project with an injected dhcp-script directive. This allows an attacker to make the host dnsmasq execute attacker-chosen code as root on a DHCP lease event and fully compromise the host.

Incorrect authorization in NIC, managed network, network zone, and ACL handling in Canonical LXD before 4.0.16, 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows an authenticated user of a restricted project or root inside an instance to manipulate host interfaces and firewall rules, read fragments of root-owned files through error messages, and disrupt or intercept other projects' networks and DNS records via unvalidated device and network configurations.

Improper authentication in the guest API connection handling in Canonical LXD before 4.0.16, 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows a root user inside an unisolated instance to impersonate another instance and read its configuration, metadata, and devices across project boundaries via holding open connections across PID wrap-around.

Incorrect authorization in backup export and network zone read endpoints in Canonical LXD before 6.10.2 allows an authenticated user with view-only access to export instance and custom storage volume backups and read network zone TSIG peer keys via endpoints enforcing only view permissions.

Exposure of sensitive information in API responses, exports, and host-side artifacts in Canonical LXD before 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows an authenticated lower-privileged user or a local host user to read credentials, private keys, and other projects' metadata and inject arguments into Ceph administration commands via unfiltered endpoints, exported configurations, log files, process command lines, and unvalidated bucket parameters.

Incorrect authorization in TLS certificate trust store and revocation handling in Canonical LXD before 4.0.16, 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows an authenticated client with a restricted or revoked TLS certificate to gain unrestricted administrative access to the server or cluster via trust-lookup races, forwarded cluster identity headers, CA-issued certificate detaching, or stale revocation and session state.

Exposure of sensitive information in token operation events in Canonical LXD before 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows an authenticated user restricted to a project to gain full server access and cancel pending token operations via capturing certificate or cluster join token secrets broadcast to default project event listeners.

Incorrect authorization in project restriction enforcement in Canonical LXD before 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows an authenticated user with restricted project access to bypass project limits and access forbidden storage pools, volumes, network addresses, and CPU resources via instance moves, backup imports with overrides, received snapshots, or unvalidated volatile keys.

Incorrect authorization in instance, snapshot, and image operations in Canonical LXD before 4.0.16, 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows an authenticated user with restricted project or per-object permissions to read and modify other clients' resources and execute arbitrary code as root on the host via missing entitlement checks on secondary objects and push-mode container migrations.

Improper privilege management during container rebuild in Canonical LXD before 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows a local user with container permissions to gain root privileges on the host via rebuilding a never-started unprivileged container so it starts without a user namespace or privileged-container hardening.

Configuration injection in virtual machine disk device handling in Canonical LXD before 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows an authenticated user with VM creation permissions in a restricted project to bypass low-level VM restrictions and control the root QEMU process via quotes and line breaks in a disk device's guest path.

Path traversal in proxy and CDI GPU device name handling in Canonical LXD before 5.0.12, 5.21.10, and 6.10.2 allows an authenticated user with access to a restricted project permitting proxy or GPU devices to read, overwrite, or delete arbitrary host files as root and terminate host processes via crafted device names containing path traversal sequences.

Path traversal in TPM device management in Canonical LXD from 4.8 before 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows a remote authenticated user with project access to recursively delete arbitrary files and directories on the host as root via a crafted device name during instance or device removal.

Configuration injection in liblxc instance configuration generation in Canonical LXD before 6.10.2, 5.21.10, 5.0.12, 4.0.16 allows an authenticated user with restricted project access or a local user of the LXD user socket to execute arbitrary commands as root on the host via line breaks in instance configuration keys and values.

Improper control of code generation and project restriction enforcement in container configuration handling in Canonical LXD before 4.0.16, 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows an authenticated user with restricted project access to execute arbitrary commands as root on the host, crash the daemon, and alter shared bridge DHCP assignments via image-supplied LXC configuration, concurrent rename races during updates, and unvalidated syscall or hardware address settings.

Path traversal in container device path resolution and VM disk format detection in Canonical LXD before 4.0.16, 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows an authenticated user with project access, including an unprivileged local user through lxd-user, to read and modify arbitrary host files or Ceph RBD images and gain root privileges on the host via crafted device paths or QCOW2 backing file references.

Untrusted search path and context handling in host-side instance helpers in Canonical LXD before 4.0.16, 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows an authenticated user with restricted project access or root inside an unprivileged container to execute arbitrary code as root on the host, read daemon memory, remount read-only shifted disks as read-write, and disrupt other projects' mounts via file API, SFTP, syscall interception, and disk hot-plug operations.

Insufficient verification of data authenticity in shared image handling in Canonical LXD before 4.0.16, 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows an authenticated user restricted to a single project to export private images, replace public image contents, remove other projects' images, and pin daemon memory via abusing fingerprint-based image sharing, partial fingerprints, and non-expiring push upload tokens.

Incorrect authorization in custom storage volume, backup, and storage bucket endpoints in Canonical LXD before 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows an authenticated user with a project-restricted certificate or per-object authorization to read, rename, move, replace, or delete other projects' storage resources and bypass cluster group restrictions via missing project or object ownership checks.

In LXD before 4.0.16, 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2, an improper limitation of a pathname to a restricted directory vulnerability allows an authenticated client restricted to a single project to write and delete files at arbitrary host filesystem paths as root.

 When a custom storage volume is pushed to a LXD daemon, the snapshot names supplied by the migration peer are never validated and are used to build the filesystem path of each received snapshot. This allows an attacker to place attacker-controlled files into any host directory as root, gaining root-level code execution on the host, and to recursively delete an attacker-chosen path.

Exposure of resource to wrong sphere in optimized ZFS backup imports in Canonical LXD before 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows an authenticated user with restricted project access to mount an attacker-controlled filesystem over arbitrary host paths and execute code as root on the host via importing a filesystem ZFS stream declared as a block volume.

Exposure of resource to wrong sphere in the instance file transfer API in Canonical LXD before 4.0.16, 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows an authenticated user with restricted project access to read and write arbitrary host block or character devices, compromise the host, and hang file transfer requests via importing device nodes or named pipes outside /dev in an image or backup and opening them on a stopped instance.

Exposure of resource to wrong sphere in image template handling in Canonical LXD before 4.0.16, 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows an authenticated user with restricted project access to read and overwrite host block and character devices via importing device nodes in an image's templates directory and accessing them through instance template endpoints.

Improper link resolution in image metadata tarball unpacking in Canonical LXD before 5.0.12, 5.21.10, and 6.10.2 allows an authenticated user with a restricted client certificate to write arbitrary host files as root and execute code on the host via a crafted rootfs symlink in an image metadata tarball.

Exposure of resource to wrong sphere in image and backup metadata handling in Canonical LXD before 6.10.2, 5.21.10, 5.0.12, 4.0.16 allows an authenticated user with restricted project access to read and overwrite arbitrary host files, access other projects' data, and block the daemon via importing device nodes, hard links, symlinks, or named pipes.

Path traversal in backup, image, storage volume, and migration handling in Canonical LXD before 4.0.16, 5.0.12, 5.21.10, 6.10.2 allows an authenticated user with restricted project access to read and write arbitrary host files as root and exhaust daemon memory via crafted symlinks, unvalidated path components, or oversized metadata.

The Android application "Tokyo Fire Department Official App" contains a path traversal vulnerability that allows a malicious application installed on a user's device to obtain sensitive information from the affected application.

A vulnerability was detected in ONNX ONNXMLTools up to 1.16.0. This affects the function get_set_node of the file onnxmltools/utils/visualize.py of the component Model Visualization. The manipulation results in cross site scripting. The attack can be executed remotely. The exploit is now public and may be used. The pull request to fix this issue awaits acceptance.

A flaw was found in wildfly-core. A management user could use the resolve-expression in the HAL Interface to read possible sensitive information from the Wildfly system. This issue could allow a malicious user to access the system and obtain possible sensitive information from the system.

cves.d: A flaw was found in spice-server. A malicious SPICE client can send a message header declaring an arbitrarily large message body. The server sizes the receive-buffer allocation from this declared size before any message content is received; when the allocation fails, the process hosting the SPICE server terminates abruptly, causing a denial of service for the virtual machine it serves. On hosts with sufficient free memory, the same technique can instead hold large amounts of memory per connection. Exploitation requires network access to the SPICE port; credential requirements depend on the server's authentication configuration.

A flaw was found in Keycloak. In Keycloak where a user can accidentally get access to another user's session if both use the same device and browser. This happens because Keycloak sometimes reuses session identifiers and doesn’t clean up properly during logout when browser cookies are missing. As a result, one user may receive tokens that belong to another user.

A flaw was found in Keycloak, where it does not correctly validate its client step-up authentication in org.keycloak.authentication. This flaw allows a remote user authenticated with a password to register a false second authentication factor along with an existing one and bypass authentication.

An **uncontrolled memory allocation** flaw has been found in the smbd_smb2_ioctl_pipe_write_done() function in source3/smbd/smb2_ioctl_named_pipe.c of the SMB2 named-pipe ioctl handling in the samba package. The file server reserves memory for a named-pipe response using a size chosen by the client. It does not keep that size within the maximum the client and the server have already agreed. A low-privileged network attacker or user who can open a named pipe can request a very large response. The file server reserves that memory before it reads the pipe and holds it until the request ends. Repeating this on more connections can exhaust memory and keep the file service unavailable while those requests continue.

A flaw was found in the HAL Console in the Wildfly component, which does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes user-controllable input before it is placed in output used as a web page that is served to other users. The attacker must be authenticated as a user that belongs to management groups “SuperUser”, “Admin”, or “Maintainer”.

cves.d: A vulnerability has been found in stylefeng Guns up to 2.2. Affected by this issue is the function TokenAndPermissionInterceptor.preHandle of the file TokenAndPermissionInterceptor.java of the component JWT Signing. Such manipulation leads to use of hard-coded cryptographic key . It is possible to launch the attack remotely. The project was informed of the problem early through an issue report but has not responded yet.

A flaw was found in Keycloak. This vulnerability enables information disclosure when the parameterized-scopes feature is enabled. The protocol mapper fails to enforce authorization checks for certain scope parameter types during token and authorization requests. An authenticated remote attacker can exploit this flaw by supplying a crafted scope parameter to retrieve sensitive profile attributes of other users without authorization.

A server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw was found in KubeVirt's decentralized live migration. The connectURL field of a VirtualMachineInstanceMigration object is not validated at admission, and the privileged synchronization-controller dials the attacker-specified URL. Connection and DNS errors from the dial are exposed in a condition readable in the tenant's namespace. A user with the kubevirt.io:migrate role (a role designed for tenant delegation) can use this behavior as a blind network-reconnaissance oracle to determine the existence and connectivity of internal hosts and ports from the controller's network vantage, including services isolated from the tenant by network policy. TLS certificate pinning prevents session completion with non-KubeVirt hosts, limiting the impact to information disclosure of internal network topology; no data content, integrity, or availability impact is possible.

A flaw was found in Red Hat Enterprise Linux's qemu-kvm virtualization software. A privileged user inside a guest virtual machine could use this flaw to make the host QEMU process copy parts of its own memory into the guest's memory, where the attacker could read it. Successful exploitation could allow an attacker to view portions of the host QEMU process memory from within a guest, potentially exposing sensitive information that could aid in further attacks. The highest threat from this vulnerability is to confidentiality.

cves.d: A flaw was found in the Dynamic Client Registration service of Keycloak, an open-source identity and access management solution. The issue occurs when a user with the view-clients role accesses the client registration endpoint to retrieve client details. Due to a failure to mask sensitive information, the service returns the client's confidential secret in cleartext. This could allow a read-only administrator to obtain full access to the affected client's account and potentially escalate their privileges within the realm.

A vulnerability was found in RPM's rpmbuild tarball processing. When processing a crafted source archive, the getTarSpec() function in tools/rpmbuild.cc passes an attacker-controlled tar archive member name to rpmExpand() as part of a %{basename:...} macro expression. A specially crafted .spec member name can therefore inject RPM macros, including Lua expressions, resulting in arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the user running rpmbuild. This can be exploited when a victim or automated build system processes an attacker-controlled source tarball using rpmbuild tarball mode (such as -ts, -ta, or -tb).

cves.d: A flaw was found in Keycloak's client registration service. A remote attacker, possessing a previously issued Registration Access Token (RAT), could exploit this vulnerability to re-enable a client that an administrator had explicitly disabled. This bypasses security controls, allowing the attacker to reset the client's secret and potentially regain privileged API access. The primary impact includes unauthorized information disclosure and potential integrity compromise.

A flaw was found in Keycloak. When revokeRefreshToken=true is enabled and persistent session storage is in use, a server restart can reset internal timing mechanisms. This allows a remote attacker, who has previously captured a user's refresh token, to replay that token even after it has been revoked. Successful exploitation grants the attacker unauthorized access to the victim's account, potentially leading to information disclosure or privilege escalation.

A flaw was found in Netty's HTTP/2 stack. This vulnerability allows a remote attacker to inject prohibited characters, such as NUL, Line Feed, and Carriage Return, into HTTP/2 header field values due to insufficient validation. When these values cross an HTTP/2 to HTTP/1.1 translation boundary, they can be exploited for request smuggling, header injection, or response splitting. This could lead to unauthorized access, data manipulation, or other security bypasses.

cves.d: A missing authorization check has been found in the find_user function in user_aware.rb of the SSH key API in the foreman package. The create action attaches a new public key to the user id in the request without checking that the caller may edit that user. A low-privileged network attacker or user who already holds permission to create SSH keys can add their key to another user's account. That key is then stored with the victim and can be used by features that export that user's SSH keys.

A missing authorization check has been found in the user_mail_notifications function in mail_notifications_controller.rb of the mail notification API in the foreman package. The action returns another user's notification settings when only the generic view permission for mail notifications is present. A low-privileged network attacker or user who can view mail notifications can request any user id and read that user's subscription choices and stored mail search strings.

A flaw was found in ansible-core's ansible.builtin.git module. The module
invokes git (ls-remote, clone, fetch) with the repository URL as a positional
argument and without a "--" separator, so a repository URL that begins with a
dash is interpreted by git as a command-line option. A caller that passes an
attacker-controlled repository URL to the module can trigger argument
injection (for example --upload-pack/--exec), resulting in arbitrary command
execution on the host running the module.

A realm administrator with the "manage-realm" role can exploit this vulnerability by submitting an arbitrary filesystem path as a keystore parameter when creating a key provider component. This allows the administrator to probe arbitrary filesystem paths, determining which files exist and are readable by the Keycloak process. This information disclosure could be used to identify high-value targets for follow-on attacks.

A flaw was found in RESTEasy's CorsFilter, which, when configured to allow all origins ("*"), reflects the request's Origin header back in the Access-Control-Allow-Origin response together with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. This permissive cross-origin policy allows a malicious website to make credentialed cross-origin requests and read authenticated responses from a victim's session, resulting in a loss of confidentiality.

cves.d: A flaw was found in rpm. A local attacker could supply a specially crafted `.gem` filename containing RPM macro syntax. When a user or automated workflow invokes `rpmuncompress -x` on this file, the macro expansion occurs during command construction. This allows the attacker to execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the invoking account, leading to a compromise of confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

cves.d: A flaw was found in SmallRye JWT's AwsAlbKeyResolver, which is used by applications to verify JSON Web Tokens signed by AWS Application Load Balancers. When the AWS_ALB key provider is configured, the resolver constructs the key-fetch URL by directly concatenating the attacker-controlled kid header value from an inbound JWT without sanitizing path traversal characters or query-string separators. This allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to force the application server to issue GET requests to arbitrary paths on the same origin as the configured key endpoint. As a result, non-public endpoints or internal data reachable on that origin may be read by the attacker before JWT signature verification takes place.

cves.d: A flaw was found in Foreman. The template revision endpoint does not enforce object-level authorization when retrieving an audited template revision. An authenticated, low privileged user with a template-related permission, such as view_ptables, can obtain historical template contents belonging to another organization or location by supplying the corresponding audit ID. This can result in unauthorized disclosure of historical template contents, which may contain sensitive configuration information, credentials, or other secrets. The REST API revision endpoints correctly restrict this lookup.

A flaw was found in hawtio-operator. The operator holds routes/custom-host:create permission cluster-wide and writes the tenant-supplied spec.routeHostName value from the Hawtio custom resource directly into the Route spec without validation or authorization checks. A namespace edit user, who normally cannot set custom Route hostnames, can use the operator as a confused deputy to claim arbitrary externally-routable hostnames, enabling subdomain takeover and, in combination with the auto-grant OAuthClient, OAuth redirect hijack.

cves.d: When Keycloak is started with `--features-disabled=account,account-api`, the Account REST API is only partially disabled. Five endpoints under the versioned path `/account/v1alpha1` remain fully functional — including both read and write operations — because they lack the `checkAccountApiEnabled()` gate that correctly blocks four other endpoints in the same REST service class. The user needs to have permissions to use the API.

A flaw was found in multicluster-global-hub. During a ManagedClusterMigration, the system incorrectly grants all managed hubs read access to a shared communication topic. This allows a compromised managed hub to intercept and collect sensitive bootstrap kubeconfigs, which contain API server tokens intended for other hubs. These tokens have an extended validity of approximately 9.86 years, significantly increasing the risk of unauthorized access and information disclosure to other managed clusters.

A flaw was found in insights-client. A compromised managed cluster, referred to as a 'spoke', can inject unencoded data into the Insights API URL path. This occurs because the ClusterID, which is controlled by the spoke, is used directly in the request path without proper validation or URL encoding. This vulnerability allows a malicious spoke to redirect authenticated requests to unintended API endpoints, potentially leading to information disclosure or unauthorized access.

cves.d: A flaw was found in Maestro. Its REST API write endpoints were registered without proper authentication middleware. This allows a remote attacker to perform unauthorized write operations, such as creating, modifying, or deleting consumers and resource bundles. This could lead to data integrity issues or a denial of service (DoS).

A flaw was found in the maestro gRPC broker. This vulnerability allows a remote attacker, with a valid client certificate, to bypass authentication. This bypass enables the attacker to subscribe to other consumers' event streams, leading to unauthorized information disclosure, or to publish forged agent status, which can compromise data integrity.

A stack out-of-bounds write vulnerability was found in gfs2-utils. In savemeta, the height value from on-disk inode metadata is used as a loop bound without bounds checking, causing a stack buffer overflow that may lead to arbitrary code execution when processing crafted GFS2 filesystem images.

cves.d: A flaw was found in Keycloak, specifically in the organization selection login page. A remote attacker with `manage-realm` or `manage-organizations` administrative privileges can exploit a Stored Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability. This flaw occurs because the `organization.alias` is placed into an inline JavaScript `onclick` handler, allowing a crafted JavaScript payload to execute in a user's browser when they view the login page. Successful exploitation enables arbitrary JavaScript execution, potentially leading to session theft, unauthorized account actions, or further attacks against users of the affected realm.

A flaw was found in Corosync. An integer overflow vulnerability in Corosync's join message sanity validation allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to send crafted User Datagram Protocol (UDP) packets. This can cause the service to crash, leading to a denial of service. This vulnerability specifically affects Corosync deployments configured to use totemudp/totemudpu mode.

cves.d: A flaw was found in openshift/oauth-proxy. On paths configured to bypass authentication (skip-auth-regex), the proxy forwards client-supplied identity headers (X-Forwarded-User, X-Forwarded-Email, X-Forwarded-Access-Token) to the upstream application without stripping them. An unauthenticated attacker can inject forged identity headers on whitelisted paths.

A flaw was found in foreman. Authenticated users with 'view_keypairs' permission can bypass taxonomy scoping, allowing them to download private SSH (Secure Shell) keys from other organizations by directly querying key pair IDs. This vulnerability leads to cross-tenant data exposure in multi-tenant deployments, potentially compromising sensitive information.

A flaw was found in Foreman. An authenticated user with host-edit permissions could exploit a cross-tenant information disclosure vulnerability. This flaw occurs because the taxonomy_scope controller method does not properly validate organization and location IDs from nested request parameters, bypassing existing authorization checks. This allows the user to leak sensitive infrastructure metadata, including subnet topology, IP ranges, gateways, DNS servers, and VLAN IDs, from organizations and locations they are not authorized to access.

A flaw was found in Foreman. This broken access control vulnerability allows an authenticated user with host-edit permissions to retarget an existing lookup value override to a different host. This is achieved by modifying the match field through nested host attributes, effectively bypassing authorisation checks. The consequence is the potential for unauthorised modification of managed host configurations across different organisational and location boundaries.

A flaw was found in Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security (ACS). An unauthenticated remote attacker can exploit a vulnerability in the login interface's OAuth callback endpoint by crafting a malicious URL. This URL, containing unvalidated `error` and `error_uri` parameters, allows the attacker to display arbitrary error messages, leading to content spoofing. Furthermore, the attacker can redirect victims to malicious domains, effectively performing an open redirect under the guise of the trusted application's user interface.

A flaw was discovered in the X.Org X server’s X Keyboard (Xkb) extension when handling client resource cleanup. The software frees certain data structures without properly detaching related resources, leading to a use-after-free condition. This can cause memory corruption or a crash when affected clients disconnect.

cves.d: A server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw was found in KubeVirt's virt-api port-forward handler. A path traversal vulnerability was identified in Samba when processing client pipe names connecting to Unix domain sockets within a private directory. Samba typically uses this mechanism to connect SMB clients to remote procedure call (RPC) services like SAMR LSA or SPOOLSS, which Samba initiates on demand. However, due to inadequate sanitization of incoming client pipe names, allowing a client to send a pipe name containing Unix directory traversal characters (../). This could result in SMB clients connecting as root to Unix domain sockets outside the private directory. If an attacker or client managed to send a pipe name resolving to an external service using an existing Unix domain socket, it could potentially lead to unauthorized access to the service and consequential adverse events, including compromise or service crashes.

An open redirect vulnerability was found in Keycloak. A specially crafted URL can be constructed where the referrer and referrer_uri parameters are made to trick a user to visit a malicious webpage. A trusted URL can trick users and automation into believing that the URL is safe, when, in fact, it redirects to a malicious server. This issue can result in a victim inadvertently trusting the destination of the redirect, potentially leading to a successful phishing attack or other types of attacks.

Once a crafted URL is made, it can be sent to a Keycloak admin via email for example. This will trigger this vulnerability when the user visits the page and clicks the link. A malicious actor can use this to target users they know are Keycloak admins for further attacks. It may also be possible to bypass other domain-related security checks, such as supplying this as a OAuth redirect uri. The malicious actor can further obfuscate the redirect_uri using URL encoding, to hide the text of the actual malicious website domain.

A flaw was found in the Openshift console. The /API/helm/verify endpoint is tasked to fetch and verify the installation of a Helm chart from a URI that is remote HTTP/HTTPS or local. Access to this endpoint is gated by the authHandlerWithUser() middleware function. Contrary to its name, this middleware function does not verify the validity of the user's credentials. As a result, unauthenticated users can access this endpoint.

A vulnerability was found in Undertow, where URL-encoded request paths can be mishandled during concurrent requests on the AJP listener. This issue arises because the same buffer is used to decode the paths for multiple requests simultaneously, leading to incorrect path information being processed. As a result, the server may attempt to access the wrong path, causing errors such as "404 Not Found" or other application failures. This flaw can potentially lead to a denial of service, as legitimate resources become inaccessible due to the path mix-up.

cves.d: A flaw was found in the Netfilter subsystem of the Linux kernel. A race condition between IPSET_CMD_ADD and IPSET_CMD_SWAP can lead to a kernel panic due to the invocation of `__ip_set_put` on a wrong `set`. This issue may allow a local user to crash the system.

A flaw was found in the IPv4 Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) classifier in the Linux kernel. The xprt pointer may go beyond the linear part of the skb, leading to an out-of-bounds read in the `rsvp_classify` function. This issue may allow a local user to crash the system and cause a denial of service.

A NULL pointer dereference flaw was found in the Linux kernel ipv4 stack. The socket buffer (skb) was assumed to be associated with a device before calling __ip_options_compile, which is not always the case if the skb is re-routed by ipvs. This issue may allow a local user with CAP_NET_ADMIN privileges to crash the system.

A vulnerability was found in Samba's "rpcecho" development server, a non-Windows RPC server used to test Samba's DCE/RPC stack elements. This vulnerability stems from an RPC function that can be blocked indefinitely. The issue arises because the "rpcecho" service operates with only one worker in the main RPC task, allowing calls to the "rpcecho" server to be blocked for a specified time, causing service disruptions. This disruption is triggered by a "sleep()" call in the "dcesrv_echo_TestSleep()" function under specific conditions. Authenticated users or attackers can exploit this vulnerability to make calls to the "rpcecho" server, requesting it to block for a specified duration, effectively disrupting most services and leading to a complete denial of service on the AD DC. The DoS affects all other services as "rpcecho" runs in the main RPC task.

cves.d: @fastify/express is the plugin that lets an application run Express middleware and Express applications inside the Fastify web framework. In versions before 4.0.14, when an application enables case-insensitive routing, middleware mounted on a path can still be skipped in two cases: a string mount path or plugin prefix containing a Unicode character whose case folding differs from a plain lowercase conversion fails to match the lowercased request path, and a matcher that stays case-sensitive inside an Express Router or application, such as a regular expression without the ignore-case flag or an explicitly case-sensitive router, only matches its own casing. In both cases a request reaches the Fastify route handler while the path-scoped middleware does not run. An attacker can use this to bypass authentication or other middleware-based access controls on the affected routes, and only applications that enable case-insensitive routing are affected. The issue is fixed in @fastify/express 4.0.14, and users should upgrade to 4.0.14 or later. As a workaround, enforce authentication in a Fastify hook such as preHandler that runs after routing, avoid such Unicode characters in mount paths, and match case-insensitively inside Express routers and applications.

@fastify/express is the plugin that lets an application run Express middleware and Express applications inside the Fastify web framework. In versions from 4.0.5 before 4.0.14, a mount path that begins with an Express 5 optional leading segment written as a group is treated as relative and has a slash prepended when it is joined to the plugin prefix, which changes what the pattern matches so the middleware ends up mounted on a path that no longer corresponds to the real request paths. The middleware therefore never runs for requests that match the intended routes, while the Fastify routes still resolve to their handlers. An attacker can use this to bypass authentication or other middleware-based access controls on the affected routes. The issue is fixed in @fastify/express 4.0.14, and users should upgrade to 4.0.14 or later. As a workaround, mount the middleware on each path spelling explicitly, or enforce authentication in a Fastify hook such as preHandler that runs after the router resolves the request.

@fastify/express is the plugin that lets an application run Express middleware and Express applications inside the Fastify web framework. In versions from 4.0.7 before 4.0.14, when middleware is mounted on a nested array of mount paths the plugin rewrites only the top level of the array, so paths inside a nested array are not adjusted for a plugin registered under a prefix and the middleware never runs for them, a nested regular-expression mount keeps its global or sticky flag and is matched statefully so it is skipped on alternating requests, a nested regular expression is not matched case-insensitively when case sensitivity is disabled, and nested dynamic paths are not covered by the earlier empty-segment check. An attacker can use any of these to bypass authentication or other middleware-based access controls on the affected routes. The issue is fixed in @fastify/express 4.0.14, and users should upgrade to 4.0.14 or later. As a workaround, flatten mount path arrays before passing them to the plugin, or enforce authentication in a Fastify hook such as preHandler that runs after the router resolves the request.

@fastify/express is the plugin that lets an application run Express middleware and Express applications inside the Fastify web framework. In versions from 4.0.3 before 4.0.14, the plugin decodes certain percent-encoded characters in the request path that Express would otherwise keep encoded, including the Unicode line separator and paragraph separator characters, and leaves them raw. A JavaScript regular expression treats those two characters as line terminators, so a regular-expression mount path that relies on the dot metacharacter fails to match a request containing them while Fastify's own router still routes the request to its handler, and the middleware mounted on that regular-expression path is therefore skipped. An attacker can use this to bypass authentication or other middleware-based access controls on routes guarded by a regular-expression mount; string mount paths are not affected. The issue is fixed in @fastify/express 4.0.14, and users should upgrade to 4.0.14 or later. As a workaround, use string mount paths, avoid the dot metacharacter in regular-expression mounts by using a character class or the dotAll flag, or enforce authentication in a Fastify hook such as preHandler that runs after the router resolves the request.

@fastify/express is the plugin that lets an application run Express middleware and Express applications inside the Fastify web framework. In versions before 4.0.14, a request with an empty dynamic route parameter reaches a Fastify route handler while middleware mounted for that path inside an Express Router or sub-application is skipped, because Fastify's router accepts an empty value where Express requires a non-empty one, and an unanchored regular-expression mount passed to the plugin is bypassed the same way. An earlier fix covered only the mount paths passed to the plugin directly, not middleware mounted inside a routed Express application. An attacker can use this to bypass authentication or other middleware-based access controls on the affected routes, with the practical impact depending on what the empty value selects in the application. The issue is fixed in @fastify/express 4.0.14, and users should upgrade to 4.0.14 or later. As a workaround, enforce authentication in a Fastify hook such as preHandler that runs after routing, mount the middleware on a static parent path, or require non-empty values in the route params schema.

A vulnerability has been found in liuwy-project zhglxt up to 3fd4ad44458f87bdad0afa997ba29706488fa1ff. This issue affects the function markdownUploadFile of the file zhglxt-web/src/main/java/com/zhglxt/web/controller/common/CommonController.java. The manipulation of the argument editormd-image-file leads to unrestricted upload. It is possible to initiate the attack remotely. The exploit has been disclosed to the public and may be used. This product is using a rolling release to provide continious delivery. Therefore, no version details for affected nor updated releases are available.

@fastify/middie is the plugin that adds Express-style middleware support to the Fastify web framework. In versions 9.3.6 through 9.3.9, a route or mount path written without a leading slash inside a plugin registered under a prefix is handled inconsistently: the middleware is mounted with a separating slash after the prefix, while the route is concatenated directly onto the prefix, so a request to the concatenated path reaches the route handler without running the middleware mounted for it. An attacker can use this to bypass authentication or other middleware-based access controls on the affected routes. The issue is fixed in @fastify/middie 9.3.10, and users should upgrade to 9.3.10 or later. As a workaround, begin all route and mount paths with a slash, or enforce authentication in a Fastify hook such as preHandler that runs after the router resolves the request.

An out-of-bounds read vulnerability was found in Samba due to insufficient length checks in winbindd_pam_auth_crap.c. When performing NTLM authentication, the client replies to cryptographic challenges back to the server. These replies have variable lengths, and Winbind fails to check the lan manager response length. When Winbind is used for NTLM authentication, a maliciously crafted request can trigger an out-of-bounds read in Winbind, possibly resulting in a crash.

cves.d: The Ultimate Bootstrap Elements for Elementor plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via multiple widgets in all versions up to, and including, 1.5.3 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping on user supplied attributes. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with contributor-level access and above, to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page.

The wpForo Forum plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'nickname / display_name (via WP core profile form); thread[body] carries the [quote data-userid=..] trigger' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 3.2.4 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with subscriber-level access and above, to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. Exploitation requires that the site administrator has disabled the profiles.mention_nicknames setting (which is off by default), causing apply_quotes() to use display_name rather than a sanitized nickname when building the data-mention attribute.

A flaw has been found in chuckfairy node-webcam up to 0.8.2. This vulnerability affects the function generateSh of the file src/webcams/FSWebcam.js of the component FSWebcam. Executing a manipulation can lead to os command injection. The attack may be performed from remote. The exploit has been published and may be used. The project was informed of the problem early through an issue report but has not responded yet.

Missing authorization in the Elastic AI Assistant for Security in Kibana can allow an authenticated assistant user to permanently delete a shared or global Security AI Assistant conversation owned by another user in the same space. The individual-delete path can treat read access to a shared conversation as permission to delete it without checking ownership. The deleted conversation history is lost to its legitimate owner.

A vulnerability was found in Undertow. This vulnerability impacts a server that supports the wildfly-http-client protocol. Whenever a malicious user opens and closes a connection with the HTTP port of the server and then closes the connection immediately, the server will end with both memory and open file limits exhausted at some point, depending on the amount of memory available. 

At HTTP upgrade to remoting, the WriteTimeoutStreamSinkConduit leaks connections if RemotingConnection is closed by Remoting ServerConnectionOpenListener. Because the remoting connection originates in Undertow as part of the HTTP upgrade, there is an external layer to the remoting connection. This connection is unaware of the outermost layer when closing the connection during the connection opening procedure. Hence, the Undertow WriteTimeoutStreamSinkConduit is not notified of the closed connection in this scenario. Because WriteTimeoutStreamSinkConduit creates a timeout task, the whole dependency tree leaks via that task, which is added to XNIO WorkerThread. So, the workerThread points to the Undertow conduit, which contains the connections and causes the leak.
